turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning. Pop yourself on the chair, I've already done the obs. Blood pressure's one twenty eight over seventy eight, pulse is eighty four, temperature thirty seven point two.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Is that high? Sorry, I'm really wound up. I saw my eyes this morning and I haven't settled since.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): That's a normal pressure, love. Nothing like my sister, hers was through the roof in January and she's on ramipril now. Yours is fine.
[SEG0004] person_3 (DOCTOR): Apologies, the login's died on me again. Two seconds. Right, what's the problem today?
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, my eyes have gone yellow. And my wee is really dark, like tea. And I'm shattered.
[SEG0006] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): We've just got back from Cornwall. We ate at those roadside stalls on the A30, the chicken and the prawn rolls. He was fine before we went.
[SEG0007] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sorry, say that again? Yellow eyes? The screen just flashed and I lost the end of it.
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Yellow, yes, both of them. It started, err, maybe four days ago, or five, I can't actually say which day.
[SEG0009] person_3 (DOCTOR): Roughly four or five days, then. And the urine, was that the same time?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, the wee went dark with it. The tiredness was a bit before that, about a week. I nearly slept through Exeter.
[SEG0011] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He was flat out on the sofa all Sunday, wouldn't touch his dinner. Still only picking at food, if I'm honest.
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): I just don't fancy anything. Is that bad? Are you going to keep me in? I was reading about livers at two in the morning and now I can't switch my head off.
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): Ignore that ping, it's another patient's alert. Any pain in the tummy? Any fever? Were you actually sick?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No pain. No fever. I felt queasy the evening we ate at the stall, but that went by the next day. It's gone.
[SEG0015] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And he doesn't drink, doctor. Not on the trip and not at home.
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): No alcohol at all?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): Never. Can't stand the taste. So it isn't the booze, is it? That's what frightened me, people saying yellow eyes means you've drunk your liver to bits.
[SEG0018] person_1 (NURSE): Sats are ninety eight percent, I'll take the probe off. Excuse me yawning, my little boy's been coughing all night, there's a bug round his nursery.
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Is ninety eight enough? I thought it had to be a hundred. And please be straight, is my liver packing up? I can take it, I just need the words.

[SEG0020] person_3 (DOCTOR): Ninety eight is normal, you don't need a hundred. The yellow in the eyes is bilirubin. When the liver's inflamed it stops clearing that pigment, so it builds up in the blood, the eyes go yellow and the wee goes dark. That is not the liver shutting down.

[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): So it is inflamed, is that hepatitis from the stalls? Dave and Priya and her boyfriend were poorly too, the runs for two days, we all ate the same prawn rolls. Am I infectious?

[SEG0022] person_3 (DOCTOR): It might be hepatitis. Hep A is the one that fits mucky roadside food. That's a working impression, provisional, the bloods have to back it up. I am not stamping a definite label on it today.

[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Does hep A go? I teach year four, do I have to stay off so I don't give it to the class? And my sister's been in the car with me, is she going to catch it? Sorry, that's a lot at once.
[SEG0024] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'm his sister, yes. I feel absolutely fine. I had the chips, not the prawns.

[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): One second, the inbox has jumped up and it isn't your result, don't panic. Most people manage this at home. I'm requesting liver blood tests and hepatitis serology, both for today downstairs. That's booked, not a maybe.
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Today, both of them? How many needles is that? What if it's hep B and it stays forever? Will they do hep E as well, the pork one? I need to know or I'll google it worse.

[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): A sharp scratch, a few bottles, that's all. Liver panel, plus hepatitis serology for A, B and C, and the acute screen should cover E. Come back and see me in a week, reception will book it before you leave. The appointment stands even if we ring sooner about an ugly result.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): A week. Right. If I go more yellow on, say, Wednesday, do I just sit tight? I won't sit tight well, I'll be a nightmare, I'm warning you.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): If you're vomiting, or confused, or the yellow races off quickly, that's A and E, don't wait. Otherwise you keep the week.
[SEG0030] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He had his appendix out at nineteen, I'll say it so it's not missed. And he's on a nose spray for his hay fever.

[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Beclometasone, two squirts each side, once a day. Been on it for years for the hay fever. I, um, left it on the bathroom shelf so I missed the whole ten days of the trip, but I'm back on it now.
[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): Carry on with that, the hay fever's ongoing and the spray's fine. Any other tablets? Paracetamol, ibuprofen, anything from the chemist?

[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Paracetamol yesterday, two tablets, five hundred milligrams each, just that once, for a headache. The headache's gone this morning. I don't take ibuprofen, it burns my stomach, but that's not an allergy, it just doesn't suit me.

[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): One dose, not a regular medicine, understood. Let me look, the window's plenty. Both sclera are yellow. Tummy's soft, not tender, I can't feel a liver edge, and there's no rash on the arms.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Not feeling the liver, is that good or bad? And is the skin yellow or only the eyes? My mum won't stop texting. I told her I'm at the GP and to leave it.
[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): Not feeling the edge is reassuring, it isn't enlarged. The skin on your chest is a bit yellow too, same pigment. I should have said, I was half on the screen.

[SEG0037] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Our mum had gallstones, she had the operation years ago. She told me to mention it in case it runs in the family. He hasn't had that colicky pain she got, I'm only passing it on.
[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): Mother's gallstones, noted. It's not the explanation I'm favouring. Any travel outside the UK, or was it just Cornwall?

[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Just Cornwall. Ten days, got back last Saturday. The stalls were near Bodmin on the way down. I feel stupid, the queue was huge, he didn't change his gloves, and I ate it anyway.
[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any pale stools? Itching anywhere?
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): No. They're brown, normal. No itching. I check the mirror about ten times a day, which is mad, I know. Will itching turn up later, should I get some cream?
[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): Don't buy cream on a guess. Have you lost weight? And how is your sleep, apart from the reading at two?
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Weight's the same, same hole on the belt. Sleep's awful though. Awake till three, heart racing, worrying I'm going to die and worrying about my class. Pathetic, I know.
[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'd put the broken sleep down to the worry, not the liver. Try and park the late night searching.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): I'll try. Is tea allowed? And fat, am I on dry toast only? I usually run on a Wednesday, is that a stupid idea now?

[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): While this request actually sends, the little wheel is just spinning. Did you hit the ring road? It was a car park from the Asda junction, and the forecast is rain all afternoon, naturally.

[SEG0047] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Forty minutes from the roundabout to your car park. We had the cricket on to stay sane. England folded before lunch again, Root nicked it and walked, and the cloud is sitting on the ground.

[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): I had it on the radio on the M5 as well. Don't know why I listen, they never bat out a session. The weather won't do that pitch any favours. Sorry, that's not why we came.
[SEG0049] person_1 (NURSE): My dad texted me the score at lunch, absolutely tragic. He'll be out in his garden in this drizzle anyway, he always is. Mad for his roses, that man.

[SEG0050] person_3 (DOCTOR): Tea is fine. No special diet, just eat what you fancy, little and often while you don't fancy much. Leave the running until you're less wiped out and we've looked at the bloods. Own towel, own cup, wash your hands, and stay off school while the eyes are yellow.
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): Own towel, stay off, got it. Thank you. Sorry I asked everything twice, I'll try not to google. See you in a week, then.

spec.situation: Person with yellow eyes, dark urine and tiredness after eating at roadside stalls on a trip; others at the trip also ill; alcohol denied; liver blood tests and hepatitis serology planned.

traps.happens: The doctor (or nurse) explains a mechanism or a diagnosis in the patient's body ('the voice box is irritated by reflux', 'diabetes dulls the nerves in the feet', 'the swelling is your body fighting infection'). A nurse or caregiver also mentions a fact about THEIR OWN life (their sister, their child, their own illness).
traps.label_rule: Explanations by the doctor are NEVER symptoms, history or social history of the patient; they may only appear as clinical_assessment or counselling if the doctor stated them as such. A nurse's or caregiver's own life facts are not recorded as the patient's. Each symptom's reported_by is the person who really described it.

features: tangent_small_talk: a long tangent or small talk (traffic, cricket, the weather, a grandchild) that holds NO clinical content; nothing from it is extracted.
doctor_misses_topics: the doctor does not ask about everything; topics never discussed are simply absent (no invented denials, no allergy line if allergies were never mentioned).
spec.doctor_style: distracted by the computer, asks for repeats

bad.reason: Poor appetite supported, but onset 'since Sunday' is only from family member, not patient.
bad.text: Poor appetite (category=gastrointestinal, status=present, onset=since Sunday, temporality=current, reported_by=patient, certainty=certain)

bad.reason: Mechanism and not liver failure supported, but certainty 'provisional' not stated for this explanation.
bad.text: Yellow eyes and dark urine are from bilirubin building up when an inflamed liver does not clear it, not from liver failure (certainty=provisional, basis=explanation of the jaundice mechanism, stated_by=doctor)

omissions.text: Reduced appetite/appetite loss was reported by the family member as 'wouldn't touch his dinner' and 'still only picking at food'.
Recent possible food exposure/travel history: returned from Cornwall; ate chicken and prawn rolls from roadside stalls on the A30 / near Bodmin; patient had only UK travel (no travel outside the UK).
Possible infectious contact/exposure history: others who ate the same prawn rolls were also unwell with diarrhoea for two days.
Negative finding asked and answered: no vomiting / was not actually sick.
Medication detail missing: beclometasone is a nose spray/nasal spray, and the patient missed it for the 10 days of the trip but has now restarted it.
Current/planned medicine use missing: paracetamol 1,000 mg once yesterday only (two 500 mg tablets) for headache; not a regular medicine.
Adverse reaction / intolerance detail: ibuprofen is not taken because it 'burns my stomach'; patient explicitly said this is not an allergy.
Investigation detail missing: hepatitis serology was specified to include A, B and C, and the acute screen should cover E; tests were to be done today downstairs and were booked, not just considered.
Follow-up detail missing: return in one week, and the appointment should still be kept even if the practice phones sooner with an abnormal ('ugly') result.
Past history detail not recorded: patient has no alcohol use ever ('never').
